title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms

paper.title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms
paper.abstract:
Abstract In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase.
At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR’s worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure H 1 ​ ( P ) H_{1}(P) is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR’s performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths.
We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent.
Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call H 1 H_{1} -balanced Successive Rejects ( H 1 H_{1} -SR).
This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules.
For Gaussian arms with common variance, H 1 H_{1} -SR achieves at least 11 / 12 11/12 of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 , and this approximation ratio converges to one as 1 − O ⁡ ( 1 / log ⁡ K ) 1-O(1/\log K) as K → ∞ K\to\infty . This is a significant improvement over original SR,
whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to 1 / 4 1/4 .
Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian
benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite
horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also
exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Best-arm identification asks how to use noisy measurements to select the alternative with the largest mean. The forecaster, who follows an algorithm, adaptively chooses which arm to measure and, after a prescribed budget of T T observations, outputs a final recommendation: its estimate of the best arm. Successive Rejects (SR; Audibert et al., 2010 ) is a particularly simple elimination algorithm that involves K − 1 K-1 phases. Each phase gives the same number of additional samples to every remaining arm, then eliminates the arm with the smallest cumulative empirical mean. The phase lengths are fixed in advance. Sequential Halving (SH; Karnin et al., 2013 ) uses a similar design but eliminates approximately half the remaining arms in each phase. These methods show that simple elimination can achieve an exponentially small probability of error. The multiplicative constant in the exponential rate, however, determines how much budget is needed when small error probabilities matter. The two methods also differ in how they use observations. Original SH ranks arms using samples collected in the current phase, whereas SR retains earlier samples in each surviving arm’s empirical mean. This distinction can affect finite-budget performance. SR remains a competitive benchmark alongside more recent algorithms such as Continuous Rejects ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and Almost Tracking ( Komiyama et al., 2026 ) . Its continued relevance raises two questions: how close is its error rate to the best attainable rate, and can a small change to its schedule close the remaining gap? The limited adaptivity of SR makes its performance gap particularly intriguing. Once the rejection rule is fixed—sample all surviving arms equally and eliminate an arm with the smallest cumulative empirical mean—the only remaining design choice is the clock : how many observations should each surviving arm have when each elimination takes place. Original SR makes one particular choice. It is not immediate whether that choice is well matched to the statistical difficulty of avoiding an erroneous elimination. We therefore study the phase schedule itself as an optimization variable. Our argument proceeds from the outside in. We first place an information bound on the H 1 H_{1} -normalized rate of an arbitrary adaptive algorithm, where the H 1 H_{1} is a popularly used complexity measure of the instance. We then restrict attention to the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules, which is a subset of all adaptive algorithms that includes the original SR, and ask for the best schedule in that class. A sharp analysis of the event that the true best arm is simultaneously below all surviving competitors turns the statistical problem into a small deterministic balancing problem. Solving it produces the phase schedule; the algorithm is a consequence of that optimization.

sections.heading: 1.1 How should we compare identification algorithms?
sections.text: An algorithm can work well when one arm is clearly better and struggle when several arms have nearly equal means. Comparing raw error probabilities across such instances confounds algorithm quality with problem difficulty. We therefore account for the gaps between arm means before comparing how quickly errors decrease with the budget. Following Komiyama et al. (2022) ; Komiyama et al. (2026) , we compare the worst-instance exponential rate after normalization by an instance complexity. We use H 1 H_{1} , the sum of inverse squared gaps to the best arm, as a complexity measure that we normalize the error rate. A larger normalized rate means a stronger guarantee relative to this measure of difficulty. Our benchmark is the best such rate over all adaptive algorithms, not just elimination methods. The algorithm does not know the true gaps; H 1 H_{1} is used to evaluate it, not as an input. This criterion does not require matching a gap-informed oracle on every instance ( Degenne, 2023 ) . We give the formal definition in Section 2.1 . Our algorithm can be used to the best-arm identification with sub-Gaussian rewards, including rewards supported in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] (or any finite region). Our optimality is for Gaussian rewards as we provides the error rate lower bound to that case.

sections.heading: 1.2 Contributions

Its unique solution gives us H 1 H_{1} -SR algorithm, that achieves the matching rate. • Comparison with all algorithms and with original SR. sections.heading: Elimination algorithms
sections.text: Beyond SR ( Audibert et al., 2010 ) and Sequential Halving ( Karnin et al., 2013 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) , Shahrampour et al. (2017) study general sequential-elimination schedules, including nonlinear cumulative phase lengths. However, they have not characterized the optimal scheduling of the phase lengths. Wang et al. (2023) develop a large-deviation analysis of adaptive identification and introduce Continuous Rejects, which dynamically chooses the phase lengths. Barrier et al. (2023) consider fixed-budget identification problems for a class of reward distributions bounded on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and consider the SR algorithm therein.

sections.heading: Minimax rates and implementable algorithms.
sections.text: Audibert et al. (2010) ; Carpentier and Locatelli (2016) show that there is an O ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) O(\log K) gap in the complexity of identifying the best arm between the fixed-budget setting (considered in this paper) and fixed-confidence settings, in which the algorithm can choose when to stop sampling. A notable difference that subsequent research disclosed is that optimization in these two settings is fundamentally different. Namely, the fixed-confidence setting allows a uniformly good algorithm. Namely, there exist several algorithms such as Track and Stop ( Garivier and Kaufmann, 2016 ) and Top-two Thompson Sampling ( Russo, 2020 ; Jourdan et al., 2023 ; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2024 ) that achieve this property, meaning they perform optimally on all problem instances, whereas in the fixed-budget setting, no such uniformly good algorithm exists ( Komiyama et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Degenne, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) . Therefore, the latter setting is closer to traditional statistical decision theory 1 1 1 Note that, in the statistical decision theory framework, it is usually called the risk measure. ( Jennison et al., 1982 ) , where the optimality depends on the choice of the complexity measure H ⁡ ( P ) H(P) , such as admissibility ( Imbens et al., 2025 ) and minimax optimality ( Komiyama et al., 2022 ) . In particular, Komiyama et al. (2022) formulate minimax rates given a complexity measure H ⁡ ( P ) H(P) , and introduce the delayed optimal tracking (DOT) algorithm. However, DOT is almost impossible to implement in practice as it needs to solve a dynamic program with a long horizon. Later on, Komiyama et al. (2026) proposed a practical algorithm called simple tracking that does not require the information on the horizon T T , and its version called almost tracking, which has a provable constant-factor rate guarantee. However, its constant on top of the rate guarantee is impractically large. Our main results start from a more practical viewpoint. Starting from the popularly used SR algorithm, we improve its performance without introducing additional complexity into the algorithm. Our main algorithm, H 1 H_{1} -SR, significantly improves the practical performance of SR, and we derive nearly minimax rate guarantees for the most popularly used complexity measure H 1 ​ ( P ) H_{1}(P) .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and limitations
sections.text: Optimizing the deterministic SR checkpoints yields H 1 H_{1} -SR, which is optimal within this class of SR-type algorithms and achieves at least 11 / 12 11/12 of the optimal Gaussian H 1 H_{1} -normalized rate for every fixed K K , with the certified fraction tending to one as K K grows; original SR approaches 1 / 4 1/4 . Experiments show substantial finite-budget gains on many instances but also a clear non-dominance case. The finite-budget bound extends to independent sub-Gaussian rewards; matching optimality beyond the Gaussian setting and the early/late elimination tradeoff remain open.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.22051v1 [stat.ML] 15 Oct 2026 Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms Mohamed Khair Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University Affiliation: of Artificial Intelligence Email: mohamed.khair@mbzuai.ac.ae Junpei Komiyama Affiliation: Mohamed bin Zayed University Affiliation: of Artificial Intelligence Affiliation: RIKEN AIP Email: junpei@komiyama.info Abstract In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase. At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR’s worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure H 1 ​ ( P ) H_{1}(P) is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR’s performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths. We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent. Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call H 1 H_{1} -balanced Successive Rejects ( H 1 H_{1} -SR). This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules. For Gaussian arms with common variance, H 1 H_{1} -SR achieves at least 11 / 12 11/12 of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every K ≥ 2 K\geq 2 , and this approximation ratio converges to one as 1 − O ⁡ ( 1 / log ⁡ K ) 1-O(1/\log K) as K → ∞ K	o\infty . This is a significant improvement over original SR, whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to 1 / 4 1/4 . Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly. 1 Introduction Best-arm identification asks how to use noisy measurements to select the alternative with the largest mean. The forecaster, who follows an algorithm, adaptively chooses which arm to measure and, after a prescribed budget of T T observations, outputs a final recommendation: its estimate of the best arm. Successive Rejects (SR; Audibert et al., 2010 ) is a particularly simple elimination algorithm that involves K − 1 K-1 phases. Each phase gives the same number of additional samples to every remaining arm, then eliminates the arm with the smallest cumulative empirical mean. The phase lengths are fixed in advance. Sequential Halving (SH; Karnin et al., 2013 ) uses a similar design but eliminates approximately half the remaining arms in each phase. These methods show that simple elimination can achieve an exponentially small probability of error. The multiplicative constant in the exponential rate, however, determines how much budget is needed when small error probabilities matter. The two methods also differ in how they use observations. Original SH ranks arms using samples collected in the current phase, whereas SR retains earlier samples in each surviving arm’s empirical mean. This distinction can affect finite-budget performance. SR remains a competitive benchmark alongside more recent algorithms such as Continuous Rejects ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and Almost Tracking ( Komiyama et al., 2026 ) . Its continued relevance raises two questions: how close is its error rate to the best attainable rate, and can a small change to its schedule close the remaining gap? The limited adaptivity of SR makes its performance gap particularly intriguing. Once the rejection rule is fixed—sample all surviving arms equally and eliminate an arm with the smallest cumulative empirical mean—the only remaining design choice is the clock : how many observations should each surviving arm have when each elimination takes place. Original SR makes one particular choice. It is not immediate whether that choice is well matched to the statistical difficulty of avoiding an erroneous elimination. We therefore study the phase schedule itself as an optimization variable. Our argument proceeds from the outside in. We first place an information bound on the H 1 H_{1} -normalized rate of an arbitrary adaptive algorithm, where the H 1 H_{1} is a popularly used complexity measure of the instance. We then restrict attention to the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules, which is a subset of all adaptive algorithms that includes the original SR, and ask for the best schedule in that class. A sharp analysis of the event that the true best arm is simultaneously below all surviving competitors turns the statistical problem into a small deterministic balancing problem. Solving it produces the phase schedule; the algorithm is a consequence of that optimization. 1.1 How should we compare identification algorithms? An algorithm can work well when one arm is clearly better and struggle when several arms have nearly equal means. Comparing raw error probabilities across such instances confounds algorithm quality with problem difficulty. We therefore account for the gaps between arm means before comparing how quickly errors decrease with the budget. Following Komiyama et al. (2022) ; Komiyama et al. (2026) , we compare the worst-instance exponential rate after normalization by an instance complexity. We use H 1 H_{1} , the sum of inverse squared gaps to the best arm, as a complexity measure that we normalize the error rate. A larger normalized rate means a stronger guarantee relative to this measure of difficulty. Our benchmark is the best such rate over all adaptive algorithms, not just elimination methods. The algorithm does not know the true gaps; H 1 H_{1} is used to evaluate it, not as an input. This criterion does not require matching a gap-informed oracle on every instance ( Degenne, 2023 ) . We give the formal definition in Section 2.1 . Our algorithm can be used to the best-arm identification with sub-Gaussian rewards, including rewards supported in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] (or any finite region). Our optimality is for Gaussian rewards as we provides the error rate lower bound to that case. 1.2 Contributions The contributions follow the same progression as the analysis. • An explicit characterization of the best rate for any adaptive algorithm. For Gaussian arms we derive an explicit upper bound R K ⋆ ≤ 1 / ( σ 2 ​ B K ) R_{K}^{\star}\leq 1/(\sigma^{2}B_{K}) on the best H 1 H_{1} -normalized rate attainable by arbitrary adaptive algorithms. • Optimization within the class of SR-type algorithms. We characterize the worst-instance rate of deterministic equal-count successive-rejection schedules. Its unique solution gives us H 1 H_{1} -SR algorithm, that achieves the matching rate. • Comparison with all algorithms and with original SR. The optimized schedule satisfies R H 1 ​ -SR / R K ⋆ ≥ B K / D K ≥ 11 / 12 R_{H_{1}	extnormal{-SR}}/R_{K}^{\star}\geq B_{K}/D_{K}\geq 11/12 for every K K , with B K / D K = 1 − O ⁡ ( 1 / log ⁡ K ) B_{K}/D_{K}=1-O(1/\log K) , whereas original SR satisfies R SR / R K ⋆ → 1 / 4 R_{\mathrm{SR}}/R_{K}^{\star}	o 1/4 as K → ∞ K	o\infty . (2017) study general sequential-elimination schedules, including nonlinear cumulative phase lengths. However, they have not characterized the optimal scheduling of the phase lengths. Wang et al. (2023) develop a large-deviation analysis of adaptive identification and introduce Continuous Rejects, which dynamically chooses the phase lengths. Barrier et al. (2023) consider fixed-budget identification problems for a class of reward distributions bounded on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and consider the SR algorithm therein. Minimax rates and implementable algorithms. (2010) ; Carpentier and Locatelli (2016) show that there is an O ⁡ ( log ⁡ K ) O(\log K) gap in the complexity of identifying the best arm between the fixed-budget setting (considered in this paper) and fixed-confidence settings, in which the algorithm can choose when to stop sampling. A notable difference that subsequent research disclosed is that optimization in these two settings is fundamentally different. Namely, the fixed-confidence setting allows a uniformly good algorithm. Namely, there exist several algorithms such as Track and Stop ( Garivier and Kaufmann, 2016 ) and Top-two Thompson Sampling ( Russo, 2020 ; Jourdan et al., 2023 ; Bandyopadhyay et al., 2024 ) that achieve this property, meaning they perform optimally on all problem instances, whereas in the fixed-budget setting, no such uniformly good algorithm exists ( Komiyama et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Degenne, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) .
